title: Dogens Intimate Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reflects on the importance of letting go of our sense of separation from the world and ourselves, a central teaching of Dogen's Zen philosophy. By embracing this idea, we can cultivate intimacy and connection with ourselves and others, and tap into a deeper reality that transcends individual experience. This process involves recognizing that our sense of self is constantly changing and releasing attachment to fixed notions of good or bad, leading to a greater presence and awareness in the present moment.

sentences.text: So the person who gives the talk gets to come up to the altar, it's really lovely, and make an offering.
Chris was helping me make an offering of incense, and I was noticing how beautiful the flowers are.
I got to make an offering earlier, but I didn't actually notice the flowers.
So it's interesting, isn't it, how little we actually notice.
Then I was thinking, what a remarkable world it is that can have such a beautiful, quiet gathering of such lovely people, and beautiful flowers.
And also giant waves that wash away school children, and nuclear power plants that are out of control.
I guess it's just getting worse, the nuclear power plants, as far as I can tell.
So much beauty, and so much suffering, and what do we do with all this?
Is there anything to do?
One response seems to be to experiment with this particular ancient form of expression.
Some way of expressing something, with our hearts, with our bodies, with our breath.
And it's so interesting because this particular form comes from Japan, right?
Where there's this big disaster, and it's sort of spreading throughout the world very, very slowly.
Here is one of maybe, I don't know, 100 or 200 Zen communities in America.
Who knows how many there are now?
When some of us started, there were probably like 10, right?
Now there's a few hundred in America.
Last week I was in Mexico, so I want to give you a little report on the state of Zen practice in Mexico.
Not a place that you right away associate with Zen Buddhist practice.
I was in the city of Jalapa, which is on the Gulf side of Mexico, in the state of Veracruz, southeast of Mexico City.
It's a bit of a thing to get there.
You fly to Mexico City, and then you take a four and a half hour bus ride.
Jalapa itself, even though it's a much larger town than Bellingham, doesn't really have a decent airport.
You can't really fly there, so that's interesting.
In the town of Jalapa, there's a Zen group very much like this one, in a kind of converted house, with a once a week sitting practice.
They have retreats four times a year.
Teachers, I think all teachers, I think they're all North American people, four teachers come in rotation each year.
They have a bit of a connection to a Zen center, or a retreat center I guess, on the Pacific side, where our guiding teacher, Norman Fischer, goes twice a year.
A place called Mar de jade.
So some people from Jalapa go across Mexico, which must be about a 10 hour bus ride, to Mar de jade for those retreats that Norman Fischer gives.
Then there are also a couple of small Zen groups in Mexico City.
Do you know Mexico City is a city of 20 million people?
You knew that?
I didn't know that.
It's a really big place.
And of those 20 million people, a few hundred practice Zen meditation.
Then there are a few groups in other lineages, just a couple.
But as far as I know, that's more or less the state of Zen in Mexico.
I was there because I knew two people who practiced in that sangha.
One is the organizer of the group, named Sergio Stern.
He's practiced a little bit at San Francisco Zen Center, and went to college in the States.
The other person I knew was a woman named Berta Laura Berridos, who came to our Samish Island sesshin, which we're having again this year in June.
We have a seven day retreat every June, at a beautiful site.
If you can come, it's really beautiful.
Anyway, it was really fun.
I thought I was pretty much staying grounded, but it does something to you to be treated like royalty for a week.
I was with my son, and we were taken to meet all the relatives and all the friends, and given wonderful meals.
We were given this apartment to stay in with nice food, all arranged.
A big bowl of mangoes.
Walker was really happy.
It's one of the few foods in Mexico he likes, his mangoes.
Lots of mangoes.
And the sangha.
I gave a talk at the Monday night practice.
I also got to lead our full moon ceremony, the Bodhisattva precept ceremony, which they had never done, because they don't have any ordained people.
Some of these forms of Zen require an ordained person in the middle.
It's kind of like the hub of the wheel or something like that, to hold that space.
So there were some things they hadn't done.
One of the people that comes once a year is Rick Spencer, who used to be in Vancouver, who is a priest we know.
He came here and gave a talk, sometime last fall.
But I guess Rick had never done too many formal Zen things.
He's done topical retreats.
So they were interested, it seemed like, in having me do some formal Zen things.
I thought you might enjoy hearing a little bit of the full moon ceremony in Spanish.
You want to hear that?
It was all written out.
My Spanish is very, very limited, but it was all written out and my pronunciation is okay, I guess.
They had never heard it.
There's a particular way that you lead this ceremony.
It's call and response.
We'll do it here next week, so you can come back and hear it in English.
The person doing the call has to understand the pattern of how you lead the chanting, in their body, and then the other people can just respond.
I was the only one who had ever done this ceremony.
I guess Berta Laro must have done it, but she didn't, I remember.
She had been a few times to San Francisco Zen Center for several months.
We had a translation worked out, and so I got to lead it.
If you know Spanish, my apologies.
If you don't, you'll be impressed.
*Homage a los siete Budas antes del Buda.
Homage a...*
Some of it's Sanskrit anyways.
*Shaka Munibu.*
Skipping into a few here.
*Homage a la sucesión de los ancestros.*
And they're all answering and the room is really full.
They've never heard this before and they're really into it.
They probably are on the whole better at singing than we are anyway.
So it was really beautiful.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
So I won't use up too much more time.
But now if we want to do it in Spanish, we've got it all figured out.
Which makes me think of one time we had a Japanese...
Rarely do we have anybody actually Japanese here in the sangha.
But I remember one time years ago we had somebody here who was Japanese, and we said, oh great, we'll do the Heart Sutra in Japanese.
That was terrible for him because it was all wrong and he didn't understand it.
It was more confusing than doing it in English.
So probably if we had really fluent Spanish speakers, it would just be hard if we did it in Spanish.
Anyway, I thought you'd enjoy hearing a little bit about that.
It was really fun.
The other thing I want to say about that, without getting too clubbish about it, is that you get to join a really wonderful international worldwide club by being a Zen student.
Anywhere you go that has a Zen practice place, you'll be welcomed.
Probably anywhere you go, anywhere in the world, if you arrive with an open heart, you'd be welcomed anyway.
But you actually believe it if you go to the Zen practice place.
So yeah, we're bowing and you can't understand everything they're saying exactly, but you understand the feeling, you understand the spirit.
I gave a talk that was translated, but I did...
Oh, something else I observed.
This was great.
I did give a talk, and mostly I would say a sentence and then Sarah would translate into Spanish.
But ahead of time I wrote out an introductory paragraph.
I thought that would be nice and polite: I'm glad to be here, and such an honor to be in a group of people who are practicing, and all this.
I wrote this out and had them double check the grammar.
I was working my way through that, and in the form of the Zen talk, you don't give a whole lot of response, right?
So even though I thought I was saying these words correctly, the grammar okay, and pronouncing them correctly, I really had no idea if they understood a thing I was saying.
In the course of this talk I interjected a few times, asking them if they understood.
They would all say, yes, yes, yes.
Then what I realized is that early on I did a few retreats with Japanese teachers who were teaching in English.
I mean, you had this experience too, right, Edie.
They often would say, do you understand?
I thought at the time it was this deep teaching.
Like, wow, they really want to know, do you really understand?
Wow, this is Zen, man.
But actually I think they just really had no idea if their words made any sense whatsoever in English, and they're just seeking reassurance.
Yeah, I don't know if Kobun would say that, but Katagiri and Kiba Roshi would always say, do you understand?
So yeah, ¿Entienden?, do you understand.
Which in a way is a great advantage.
I think Norman talks a lot about how it's really helped his ability to present Dharma, to give these talks in another country, because you have to speak more simply and more clearly.
I was reflecting that my talks tend to be long and complicated.
So I've made a resolution, a post-Mexico resolution, to be a little more simple, a little more clear.
It would help my practice too, to try to express things simply.
I was telling somebody that oftentimes after I give a talk, people say, oh, that was really interesting, lots to think about.
And they realize, that's probably not too good.
It's entertaining, I guess.
Is it useful?
Is it useful?
So I gave a talk there about Dogen, and I gave a similar talk in Seattle.
I'm like a rolling stone here, giving the same talk in three different places.
So I want to give it here also.
I've been trying to re-engage with Dogen.
Dogen is the 13th century Japanese priest who is credited with being the founder of this school.
I guess historically he more or less is.
Religious history is wonderfully revisionist anyway, but he pretty much is.
Dogen was unusual because he wrote a lot.
Most Zen teachers don't write that much, especially in Kamakura Japan.
It was mostly just spoken and lived teaching.
So Dogen wrote a lot, and somehow his writing, pretty much all of it as far as we know, survived.
For several hundred years it wasn't really studied.
There was a revival of Dogen recently.
So we have this great body of writing from the founder of the school, from 1200 to 1252 were his dates.
So very old.
How could this still be relevant to us?
And difficult in some ways to read, because Dogen was not interested in something that was simple.
He was interested in, how do we actually understand this life?
How do we actually live faced with flowers and nuclear disasters?

When you first look at the way he expresses himself, and of course we're reading him in translation, and there in Mexico they're studying Dogen in a Spanish translation of the English translation of the Japanese, the modern Japanese, which is a translation of the archaic Japanese.
So it's interesting.

Anyway, I've gradually come to realize that even though Dogen at first seems hard to understand, with lots of paradox, lots of juxtapositions, lots of reversals, saying one thing means another thing, and the same thing means the opposite, all this seems to actually not revolve around being difficult or being scholastic or needing to be like really smart.

That sort of unfeeling more and more actually has to do with intimacy, with connection, with really feeling what we're feeling and being in touch in some way with something that we forget we're not always in touch with.

Because I think we come to this practice looking for something, trying to find something, and maybe we aren't really clear what's missing, but there's a sense, isn't there, that something is not quite complete in my life.
Something's not right.
Something's not quite adding up.
And it might be that there's some sort of internal problem or limitation, something we're aware of, that we would like to work with in our practice, that we have identified with our little brain.
Maybe we want to be calmer or kinder.
Because all of us have tried out the simple formulas for happiness that were offered to us by our culture and our upbringing, right?

And given that we are living in one of the most privileged cultures in the world, although nothing to say we won't have a huge problem tomorrow and Bellingham won't be washed away, but at the moment we have this incredibly privileged society that we're in the middle of.
So if the basic formula we were given actually was true, wouldn't it be the case that we would just be deliriously happy all the time?
I mean, we have food to eat, shelter, a place to come to like this.
It's incredible.
I think there's some sense of separation, some kind of distance between us and the world, some sort of isolation even in the middle of a crowd of friends like this.
And I think that's what Dogen was really interested in.
How can we turn that inside out?
Is that really real, this sense of separation?
Thinking about that made me think of a lot of things, but one of the things I thought about the other day was, do you remember that wonderful movie?
It's actually from 1971, called Harold and Maud.
Do you know that movie, Harold and Maud?
Do younger people know that movie?

Anyway, in that movie, you remember, there's a young narcissistic character, Harold, who's basically us, and he's falling in love with this really vivacious, bigger than life, wonderful older woman named Maud.

Everyone's favorite scene in that movie is there at a carnival or something, and she's just so naturally engaging with the world, and he sees this, and he says to her, "You're really good with people, aren't you?"
And she says, in this wonderful accent, which I won't try to do, "Well, why wouldn't I be?
They're my species."
So there's a sense that we don't really feel a part of our own species.
There's that sense of not belonging, not quite belonging.
I have a long, interesting background about Dogen, which I will skip, trying to keep to the point.
I want to just bring up a few particular phrases from Dogen, a few teachings from Dogen.
One of the writings he's famous for is a big collection of essays called Shobogenzo.
It translates to *The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye*.
Over the course of his life, he wrote this series of essays that have been collected in different ways.
He wrote lots of other stuff, too, but this is the most famous.
What's wonderful for us, actually, about Dogen now: the first translation of Dogen in English was not made until the 1970s, about the same time as Harold and Maud, actually.
But since then, there have been several translations, each one in some way probably a little better than the last.

And just recently, just this year, two wonderful scholars working with lots of others and teachers completed a translation of this whole book of essays, which has been translated completely in English before, but this is probably the best translation yet.
So it's a great time to be interested in Dogen, because he's more accessible than he was.

I wanted to just highlight a few phrases from probably the best known essay in this book of essays, Shobogenzo, which is called Genjokoan, which is translated in this book as "actualizing the fundamental point."
So what is the fundamental point of our life?
How do we bring that to life?
Here are three phrases from Genjokoan.
In some way I think these all speak to this question of separation, and how do we respond to that, and how are we in some way recreating and solidifying that in the way we think about things.
The first one is:
*To carry oneself forward and illuminate myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forth and illuminate the self is awakening.*
Some of the language, you know, is not the way we usually talk, so listen to that again.
*To carry oneself forward and illuminate myriad things*, the universe, *is delusion*, is delusion.
*That myriad things come forth and illuminate the self is awakening.* So that's interesting, the sense of who's in the driver's seat.
The second one is very famous, and that is:
*To study the way of enlightenment is to study the self.
To study the self is to forget the self.
To forget the self is to be actualized by myriad things.
When actualized by myriad things, your body and mind, as well as the bodies and minds of others, drop away.
No trace of enlightenment remains, and this no trace continues endlessly.*
So there are those myriad things again.
It's a little more complicated and it sounds like a series, so here that is again.
*To study the way of enlightenment is to study the self.
To study the self is to forget the self.
To forget the self is to be actualized by myriad things.
When actualized by myriad things, your body and mind, as well as the bodies and minds of others, drop away.
No trace of enlightenment remains, and this no trace continues endlessly.*
So again, it's very similar, right?
This sense of an interplay with the universe.
And then the last one I want to mention is a short one:
*When you first seek Dharma, you imagine you are far from its environs.
At the moment when Dharma is authentically transmitted, you are immediately your original self.*
This sense of turning on its head the idea that maybe we have to work hard and learn lots of stuff until we get to some place.
Maybe we're already there.
So all three of these teachings are along the same lines.
And I'll say a few words about them, most of which I hope you'll be able to hear.
So the first one is to study the way of enlightenment is to be actualized by myriad things.
I'll say a few words about them, most of which I hope you'll forget, which is okay.
But what can be interesting about these teachings is just to see if any of these phrases catch you.

And there may be some way that you can bring them up and work with them and study them as a support in your own life for this process of softening or shedding this sense of separation that we've created, so that we can fully be in the world, alive, and be able to help.
And all but [unclear: "all three of you"] seem to address this big idea we have, very big idea we have, of a self, of me.
And that we have this sense of improving or clarifying this self.
So Dogen maybe is saying something about maybe there's some way of relaxing about that.
That instead of improving and fixing, maybe there's some way of softening or dropping this idea, as useful as it is.
It's useful, but does it really serve us well?
And maybe in some way allowing others in more fully, the universe in.
Or maybe taking a fresh look at this very strong idea that, you know, there's me over here and you over there.
Is that really the case?
I mean, it's conventionally true, obviously.
But in some deeper way, is that really the case?
An analogy this makes me think of is a very common analogy of waves, waves in the ocean.
This separate being that we think of as the self, another way to think about it maybe is, what if this separate self is like a wave in the ocean?
Now you can look at a wave in the ocean.
You can see there's one wave.
There's another wave.
They seem to be different.
But it's really just one ocean, right?
What is the exact point where the wave stops and the ocean begins?
Is it this molecule, that molecule?
And what happens when the wave rides up onto the shore and is reabsorbed by the ocean?
Does the wave die?

So this first phrase from Dogen, *to carry oneself forward and illuminate myriad things is delusion*, maybe would be like the wave thinking to the wave's little self, "I'm just going to go up there on that white, sandy place there and see what it's like.
I'll report back."
Never to be seen from again.
Heard from again.
And so it seems that Dogen's not saying, "Well, fix yourself up and then you'll get enlightenment."
There seems to be some sense here of releasing into something.
So then the second, longer teaching is pretty interesting, I think.
And this is actually all I had time to speak about in Mexico.
Might have been better off there.
This thing about studying the self and forgetting the self.
So the first line is just where we all start, I think.
It makes perfect sense to us, right?
*To study the way of enlightenment is to study the self.* This is like inner work, right?
There's about a million books at the self-help bookstore about this.
We want to get to know the self better.
We realize that we've been running around and kind of lost in some sort of haze of productivity and maybe some level of self-denial.
So we want to study the self.
That's a good idea.
But then right away he turns that upside down and we're not sure what to do.
He says, *to study the self is to forget the self.* So what does that mean?
Is that some sort of denial of our consciousness?
Is it all just a big mistake to think that there's some person named Tim or Dallas or Chris or [unclear: "Alvors"]?
Was it all just a dream?
And is there something wrong with us?
Are we like bad people? [unclear: "All leaving your self."] Is that what he's saying?
I don't think so.
But what he's saying might be, maybe that's a better word than forget, maybe there's some possibility here of a release from our agenda based on such limited information.

So much of what we think about the world is actually an interpretation, isn't it, if we really look carefully at the process of consciousness, and meditation practice gives us some tools in space where that's possible.

In Mexico I gave an example, they liked this example, which is, say you're walking down the street and a friend of yours is walking on the other side of the street in the opposite direction and you wave and stuff but they don't look up.
They don't say hello.
So right away you have all kinds of stories, right?
Is she mad at me?
Oh, maybe that email I sent last week.
Maybe the tone didn't go over quite right.
And of course you don't actually know, but this idea which is created by self is so real.
It's so real when you believe in it.
So perhaps that's part of what Dogen is bringing up here.
Can you forget these stories, these ideas that are generated, which are actually based on very limited information?

One of the things I like to do is notice, just walking around, or the gym is really good for this, the way just from the slightest teeny little bit of sensory information you can make incredible stories about people, right?
Just the slightest shape of their body, you know what I mean?
You know what kind of person they are right away, you know?
What I mean?
Or just the way they look or the way they move their hand or something?
All these stories.
These stories are so real and so immediate and so much a part of how we create this self.
So maybe forgetting the self is some sense of taking a fresh look at this constant regeneration of the self.
What's really happening?
And can we relax a little bit about it?
Of course sometimes we can and sometimes we can't.
There's this sort of sense of opening when conditions are right.
Is that forgetting the self?
Maybe.
And constricting when conditions lead to constriction, when we're upset, when there are problems.
I think it would be a mixed understanding of practice, and just another way of beating ourselves up, to feel like we're a bad person when we're constricted, you know what I mean?
No, it's just a natural result of conditions, because it all comes out of what's actually happening.
So it might be that this forgetting the self includes a broad process of opening and exploring, inquiry.
Oh, that was just a story.
Wow, fantastic.
And oh, I hate this.
And suffering.
Sometimes we say in Zen, your best teacher is your suffering, which is why we don't have enormous turnouts at retreats.
But it's really true.
If you want to just feel nice and ignore your suffering, you can do that for a while.
If that works for you for the rest of your life, fantastic, have a nice time.
But it might not.
So this forgetting the self, I think, is a pretty broad process.
Someone came to me the other day and said, "I'm really glad you're bothered about teaching me, because I have so much trouble forgetting myself."
That's not exactly what he means.
Is there a self that can forget the self?
But then it gets very lovely, because he says that in this process, in this forgetting, in this softening of the self, there's a sort of awakening.
They use the word actualized.
So, brought to life, maybe.
Made truly real.
Actual means real, right?
Actualized, made real.
To forget the self is to be actualized by myriad things.
Now this would be easy to misunderstand because of our incredibly powerful apparatus of preference, right?
We would like to be actualized by the parts of the world that we like.
We would not like to be actualized by the parts of the world that we do not like.
And this includes all that as well.
I was noticing in my own little experience of going to Mexico and being treated so wonderfully.
I didn't have any more responsibilities.
They just told me what to do and where to go.
Everyone was so nice, and on their best behavior and all that.
So I was feeling very relaxed and very soft about the self.
Oh, how nice.
And then I came home, right?
As you do.
Right away there were problems.
A dear drama friend gave me some criticism, which I couldn't ignore.
It was actually probably true.
And then I felt the self just like, ah!
And then like, ah!
Is this part?
That's also part of this.
That's also part of this.
But neither is exactly real either in the way we think it is.
You are neither a wonderful enlightened being in those moments when you feel good, nor are you a complete schmuck when someone points out to you the fact that you're a little bit stuck on yourself.
Because of course you are.
That's how the self works.
There would be no self if you weren't stuck on yourself.
So what's wrong with that?
That's this process of actualization.
I read this the other day, so maybe I'll read it again because we have time.
There's this lovely poem from Rumi.
Do you remember this poem called Bird Wings?
Yeah, let's hear it.
You want to hear that poem again?
Yeah, it's the last poem about this process of forgetting the self.
I don't know why all of a sudden we're forgetting Buddhism and into Sufi wisdom, but that's okay.
*Your grief for what you've lost lifts a mirror up to where you are bravely working.
Expecting the worst, you look, and instead here's the joyful face you have been wanting to see.
Your hand opens and closes and opens and closes.
If it were always a fist or always stretched open, you would be paralyzed.
Your deepest presence is in every small contracting and expanding.
The two as beautifully balanced and coordinated as bird wings.*
*Your grief for what you've lost* — and what have we lost?
We've lost everything.
*Your grief for what you've lost lifts a mirror up to where you are bravely working.
Expecting the worst, you look, and instead here's the joyful face that you've been wanting to see.
Your hand opens and closes and opens and closes.
As if it were always a fist or always stretched open, you would be paralyzed.
Your deepest presence is in every small contracting and expanding.
The two as beautifully balanced and coordinated as bird wings.*
So this deep presence, right there, right there.
That's what Dogen's talking about too.
And then when you are actualized by myriad things, he says, your body and mind, as well as the bodies and minds of others, drop away.
This dropping away of body and mind was kind of a stock phrase in Dogen.
It seems to be his way of talking about release and awakening.
For me it has an actual element of lived experience, felt in the body.
Maybe you know this feeling that I'm talking about.
There's a feeling, when we settle into meditation practice, that it all can just drop away.
Of course, he's talking about something broader than what we can conceptualize or talk about.
But it's not just an idea or something floating in space.
It's a lived experience in the body and in the mind.
What's interesting here is he says, this is not just you.
This is not just you.
We come to practice wanting to feel better, but he says, well, it's not just that you're going to feel better.
The effect of you engaging in this release supports everyone else, helps everyone else.
I think we all know that from experience.
If you get to spend time with somebody, a dear friend or a teacher or a mentor, when they're pretty grounded, pretty settled, you feel something, you really feel something.
There are lots of theories now in neurology that somehow your neurons are maybe even lining up.
But still, it's not just you.
So we're not another sort of pointer to the sort of non-separation between us.
This can really inspire us.
This can really help us return to practice and return to our deepest intentions for how we're going to live, because we can remember that it's not just for us.
This is not a greedy, self-focused thing.
It helps everybody.
And the effect of this is so broad, he says, broader than we can understand, because he ends this little teaching with, no trace of enlightenment remains.
No trace of enlightenment remains.
And this no trace continues endlessly.
So there's something that just spreads throughout the universe, some non-something.
No trace.
This is really helpful because we really want something.
We want something to hold onto.
And it's upsetting, it's difficult, that there's nothing to hold onto, and nobody we can really rely on.
This is what Buddha's original problem was, right?
You know the story of the Buddha, that he was sequestered and given all the wonderful stuff that's supposed to make you happy.
But somehow he wasn't quite content.
He recognized that everybody's going to get sick.
Everybody's going to die.
There's nothing, nobody you can depend on.
Everything's falling apart.
How can you live?
So it's a big spiritual question.
And Dogen's saying, yes, isn't that wonderful?
No trace remains.
Can you appreciate that?
So it's wonderful and horrible, right?
The opening and closing of these bird wings, the flowers and the nuclear disaster.

The last of these three teachings from Dogen I want to mention, and then I'll wrap it up and we can talk a little bit together, is really important because we're great at making projects with things, aren't we?
We're great project people.
We know how to make a list.
We know how to cross things off.
We may on some level recognize how much we suffer from this, but it works for us.
So we'll make a new list.
Maybe this time we'll cross them all off, right?
We're great project people, and I speak from experience here.
I'm very much a project kind of person.
We bring that attitude to our spiritual life, right?
We bring that attitude to our relationships, and we bring that attitude to everything.
We want to know, how can I get this done?
How can I make it better?
How can I finish it as quickly as possible so I can go into what I really want to do?
Which is, I'm not sure, but something not this.
This last teaching from Dogen is kind of a corrective to that.
Don't make practice into a project.
When you think that practice is a project, you think you're far away from something.
You think there's something over there to get or accomplish.
So he said, *when you first seek Dharma, you imagine you're far away from its environs.

And at the moment when Dharma is authentically transmitted, you are immediately your original self.* This was a very central point to Dogen's thought, which is to be a little skeptical of this idea that I'm a mess over here and there's enlightenment over there that I'll get later.
Maybe these two things can completely coexist.
You're both a mess and you're perfect.
There's both delusion and enlightenment right here.
So the process is more a process of recognition.
Awakening, meaning to awaken to what actually is the way things really are.
